The following page provides a reference to resources that can guide countries in adapting the guidelines for country use. To implement WHO recommendations in country settings, governments must interpret and then adapt the content in line with local policies, procedures, and digital tools. This implementation guide provides the generic content required in digital systems, independently of a specific software application and with the intention that countries can adapt it to meet local needs. WHO guidelines articulate and endorse rigorously tested recommendations for health interventions to be adopted within country programs. When applied correctly and consistently, guideline recommendations save lives. To ensure that countries can effectively benefit from digital health investments, the SMART Guidelines approach is intended to facilitate the accurate reflection of WHO’s clinical, public health and data use guidelines in the digital systems that countries are adopting. For more on layers of knowledge representation and how they are used in WHO’s SMART Guidelines approach, see WHO’s SMART Guidelines and this Lancet article00038-8/fulltext). The standards-based technical artifacts in this implementation guide are at the third layer of knowledge representation (L3: Machine-readable recommendations). It provides code necessary for software developers to incorporate standardised logic from WHO guidelines into digital systems, testable for conformance to standards including fidelity to recommendations. A standards-based technical implementation guide builds on operational (L2) by mapping L2 content to value sets and Health Level Seven International Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) standards. Alongside data standards from L2, this allows for semantic and syntactic interoperability at scale. The logic derived from guidelines, which might include clinical decision support and calculations for performance indicators, which may be encoded into Clinical Quality Language (CQL). This ensures that key indicators can be consistently extracted to support patient care, as well as case surveillance and programme monitoring. The machine-readable representations in this implementation guide are intended for adaptation into countries’ digital health service delivery and reporting systems. Digital solutions comprising L3 machine-readable recommendations may then be testable for conformance to interoperability standards. The fourth layer (L4: Executable—reference applications and services) focuses on software applications and services within a digital ecosystem. It is intended to include executable reference software that accurately represents the intentions, operational, and functional requirements of the WHO recommendations; addresses user and health system needs; and comprises machine-readable data and calculations within interoperability standards, as documented in the L1–L3 layers. As a fully functional application, it is intended to serve as a generic starting point, ready to be localised to the specific operational context of the users, population, and health system within which it is deployed. Additional products at this layer include terminology services to support consistent data representation for interoperability; reusable software libraries including software development kits; application programming interfaces; and function as a service to support updates to FHIR content and capabilities across subscribed digital systems.

This page describes the core business processes and workflows for the Personal Health Wallet (PHW) Implementation Guide, integrating IHE IT Infrastructure Privacy Consent on FHIR (PCF) v1.1.0 ( https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/1.1.0/ ) and IHE IT Infrastructure Verifiable Health Links (VHL) v1.0.0-comment ( https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/1.0.0-comment/ ). A business process is a set of related activities or tasks performed together by system actors and human personas to achieve a health information exchange objective. Each workflow below is authored in BPMN 2.0 ( input/business-processes/PHW.A.bpmn , input/business-processes/PHW.B.bpmn , input/business-processes/PHW.C.bpmn ) with full BPMN Diagram Interchange ( bpmndi:BPMNDiagram ) layout and drawn from it to SVG ( input/images/PHW.A.svg and so on) by tools/render-bpmn/render bpmn.ts ; never edit a drawing, change the BPMN. The data sharing agreement processes D to H, below, take the same form. Architectural Principles 1. Trust-Anchor Neutrality : Every process models PKI key publication ( [ITI-YY1] ) and trust list retrieval ( [ITI-YY2] ) against an abstract Trust Anchor actor ( https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/ActorDefinition/TrustAnchor ). The WHO Global Digital Health Certification Network (GDHCN) is one possible Trust Anchor implementation among others (such as national health PKI roots, regional cross-border trust networks, or bilateral federation anchors). 2. Explicit IHE PCF and VHL Transaction Binding : Every cross-actor task names its normative IHE transaction ( [ITI-108] Access Consent, [ITI-YY1] Submit PKI Material with DID, [ITI-YY2] Retrieve Trust List with DID, [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL, [ITI-YY4] Provide VHL, [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest). 3. No IHE IUA Claim : Consent management and enforcement operate over IHE PCF [ITI-108] Access Consent and VHL [ITI-YY1] – [ITI-YY5] without claiming conformance to IHE Internet User Authorization (IUA [ITI-71] ). 4. Three-Valued Consent Decision and PROV-O Provenance : During VHL redemption (Process C), patient privacy consent directives retrieved via [ITI-108] are translated to W3C ODRL 2.2 policies ( consentToOdrl() ) and evaluated via three-valued decide() ( permit deny unknown ), recording a W3C PROV-O prov:Activity citing Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId . data sharing agreement (DSA) between a data provider and a data recipient. Each one is a technical process from the DSA process analysis for folio-assistant 2702 (P4, P5, P11, P12 and P13). The owner chose this IG as their home on 2026-10-30 (19:59Z). They apply to every agreement, whether it is computable (a W3C ODRL 2.2 Agreement derived from the legal text) or document-only (a signed PDF). The only difference is where the access rule comes from: the ODRL Agreement , or a configuration an administrator sets by hand from the PDF. What every process relies on: The agreement's fixed-version URL. Each agreement version is published at an immutable URL, with its SHA-256, and catalogued as a DCAT 3 dcat:Distribution with spdx:checksum (DCAT 3 §6.8, §6.8.20). For a computable agreement this URL is also the ODRL uid . Tokens, grants, Consents and audit records cite this URL, never a "latest" URL. Grants are W3C Verifiable Credentials 2.0. A grant cites the agreement through relatedResource (VC DM 2.0 §5.3), and its status is a W3C Bitstring Status List entry. litlfred/smart-trust-tools verifies it. Pluggable trust anchors. WHO GDHCN is one option. The others are a national X.509 PKI, the party's own did:web , or a local list. UDAP, as profiled by HL7 SSRAA, is approved (owner, 2026-10-30 20:28Z) for X.509 certificate-based registration and authentication, which fits a national X.509 PKI as the anchor. OpenID Federation is out of scope . No invented fields. Where no standard has a slot, the text says so as a gap or open point . It applies the business processes A, B, C, F and I of this guide to one case: the IPS Pilgrimage (Hajj) implementation guide ( smart-ips-pilgrimage , FHIR R4, IHE PCF 1.1.0). It follows the analysis written for folio-assistant 2702 on 2026-10-30. The case: during Hajj, the host country (KSA) is the VHL Receiver . It asks the pilgrim's origin country (for example Malaysia) for the pilgrim's International Patient Summary (IPS) over a Verifiable Health Link (VHL). The origin country's health information exchange (HIE) is the VHL Sharer . The IPS carries two consent statements from the pilgrim, and those two Consents are the policy for the exchange. The page does not change the IPS Pilgrimage guide. The gaps below say what that guide, or the specifications it uses, would need. Gap G1 has since been resolved in that guide by smart-ips-pilgrimage 3. The pilgrim's consents are the policy For Hajj, there is no separate data sharing agreement for the Sharer to look up. The pilgrim's two Consents are the policy, and each is coded in Consent.policyRule (owner, Q-DRAIN-5, 2026-11-01 07:44Z). That is how the IPS Pilgrimage guide models them since smart-ips-pilgrimage 3. policyRule holds a code from that guide's IPS.HAJJ.CONSENT CodeSystem, with coding.version set to the CodeSystem version whose consent text the pilgrim was shown. Any arrangement between KSA and the origin country, such as a memorandum of understanding, stays outside the computable decision. Gap What is missing What would close it --- --- --- G1. The Hajj consents are not computable as written. Resolved by smart-ips-pilgrimage 3. Was: the consent type sat in provision.purpose , the examples had display names only, and policyRule.text was "some policy" , so decide() would return unknown every time. Still open in that guide: the consent texts for two origin countries ( CONSENT-IDN , CONSENT-OMN ) are placeholders (consent rule 3). HajjConsent now requires policyRule with an IPS.HAJJ.CONSENT code and coding.version (CodeSystem version 2.1.0). policyRule also satisfies R4 invariant ppc-1 , so no policy.uri is needed. It also requires provision.actor (an Organization by identifier, role IRCP ), provision.purpose from v3 PurposeOfUse ( TREAT ), and provision.period . See the examples below. G2. Which copy of a consent counts. The specifications do not say whether the Sharer enforces the registry copy or the copy inside the IPS, or what KSA should do with its copy. A rule in the implementation guide, not a new field: the Sharer enforces the registry copy (PCF [ITI-108] ); the IPS copy is evidence, carrying its meta.versionId so that KSA can cite it. G3. mTLS is not a VHL option. The IPS Pilgrimage guide's sequence diagram still authenticates the KSA node with mTLS ( [ITI-19] ). Since smart-ips-pilgrimage 3, its transaction page says that mTLS is not one of VHL [ITI-YY5] 's three options and recommends OAuth with SSRAA. How KSA's certificate or key is published in the ips-pilgrimage trust domain is still not specified. Choose one VHL option: OAuth with SSRAA (UDAP) , approved for process D and I, which is X.509-based like mTLS; or HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421). KSA publishes the matching key in the trust domain ( [ITI-YY1] ). G4. The facility and the clinician are invisible. CONSENT-KSA is limited to healthcare facilities in the Hajj district, but the request comes from one national KSA EMR. With HTTP Message Signatures, the Sharer sees only KSA, so it cannot check the district limit and the audit cannot name who looked. HL7 SSRAA: the hl7-b2b extension carries organization id and the requesting user (SSRAA §5.2.1.1). G5. The purpose of use is not carried. [ITI-YY5] has no purpose parameter, so the decision assumes TREAT from the Consent's provision.purpose . This is open point 3 of process I. HL7 SSRAA purpose of use in hl7-b2b (SSRAA §5.2.1.1), with HL7 v3 PurposeOfUse codes. G6. KSA's duties after receipt are not machine-readable. CONSENT-KSA allows "any follow up care" and says nothing about retention or onward sharing. Nothing in VHL, IPS or PCF carries such obligations with the document. Either HL7 Data Segmentation for Privacy (DS4P) obligation codes in meta.security ( needs owner approval : not final), or, with approved standards only, KSA keeps following the CONSENT-KSA text it is bound by and audits against it in process G, with no labels on the document. That guide now states it, as process I gives it ( PHW.I.9 ): the Consents by policyRule code and CodeSystem version, each Consent's id and meta.versionId , receiver, purpose and documents released or the refusal. KSA, as an ATNA Secure Node (VHL Vol 1 §1:XX.3), also audits what it receives. IHE BALP patterns need owner approval. G8. Break the glass has no VHL. In phase 2 of the IPS Pilgrimage guide (process 5.0) the pilgrim may be unconscious: no QR code and no passcode, so the lookup is by pilgrimage number, outside VHL entirely. Its own search transaction (likely IHE PDQm [ITI-78] with IHE MHD [ITI-67] ), a separate opt-in Consent (the wallet's "break the glass" setting), and the emergency purpose of use ETREAT . It describes the VHL steps in its own transaction pages, partly in older SMART Health Links wording ("modified ITI-67"). Summary This implementation guide specifies how a Personal Health Wallet (PHW) lets a person record privacy consent, share health information through verifiable health links, and have that consent enforced when the information is used. It uses IHE Privacy Consent on FHIR (PCF) 1.1.0 for consent directives and IHE Verifiable Health Links (VHL) 1.0.0-comment for the links. Every process is trust-anchor neutral : keys are published to, and trust lists read from, an abstract Trust Anchor. The WHO Global Digital Health Certification Network (GDHCN) is one possible Trust Anchor among others. The guide makes no claim of conformance to IHE Internet User Authorization (IUA). Supporting guidance, recommendations, resources and standards are listed in the Bibliography and on the Dependencies page. What this guide contains Business Processes : eleven BPMN 2.0 processes: Consent and verifiable health links: A record and manage consent, B issue a consent-backed link, C present and redeem a link. Data sharing agreements between servers: D register a client, E server-to-server access, F access decision, G audit and provenance, H revocation and suspension, I decide a link request under an agreement. Shared certificate processes: J issue a certificate, K verify a certificate and its status. Decision-support Logic : the DMN decision PHW.DT.AgreementAccess , which combines several agreements for one receiver. This page lists the roles the business processes of this guide name, and the example people and systems that play them. Every person is fictional. Roles Role Played by Description --- --- --- Holder person The person who holds a Personal Health Wallet, records consent, and presents verifiable health links and certificates. Specializes the ActorDefinition Holder (input/fsh/actors/actors.fsh). Consent Recorder person, system The person or system that records a consent directive for the holder (IHE PCF Consent Recorder): the wallet itself, or a health worker on the holder's behalf. Consent Registry system Holds consent directives and answers IHE PCF [ITI-108] Access Consent. Specializes the ActorDefinition ConsentRegistry (input/fsh/actors/actors.fsh). VHL Sharer system Holds the health information, generates verifiable health links, and enforces consent when a link is redeemed. Specializes the ActorDefinition Issuer (input/fsh/actors/actors.fsh). VHL Receiver system Receives a verifiable health link, checks its signature against the trust list, and retrieves the information. Specializes the ActorDefinition Receiver (input/fsh/actors/actors.fsh). Trust Anchor system Publishes the trust list of keys that participants use to check signatures. GDHCN is one possible anchor among others. Specializes the ActorDefinition TrustNetworkAnchor (input/fsh/actors/actors.fsh). Certificate Issuer person, system A health worker or issuing system that issues a verifiable digital health certificate. Specializes the ActorDefinition Issuer (input/fsh/actors/actors.fsh). Verifier person, system Checks a certificate and its status, with or without a status checking application. Specializes the ActorDefinition Receiver (input/fsh/actors/actors.fsh). Data Provider Administrator person The person at a data provider who registers clients under a data sharing agreement. Data Recipient System system A server that accesses data under a data sharing agreement (OAuth client) and performs the agreement's duties. Provider Authorization Server system Registers clients and decides access under a data sharing agreement (policy decision and enforcement). Auditor person The person who reviews audit and provenance records under a data sharing agreement. Example people Ana (data provider administrator) Persona: the administrator who registers partner servers under the data sharing agreements her health information exchange signs. Fictional. Roles: Data Provider Administrator. Goal. Register only the clients an agreement allows, and revoke them the moment it ends. Needs The agreement's terms in a form the server can check One place to suspend a client Frustrations Agreements that exist only as PDFs Dr Mei (receiving clinician) Persona: an emergency physician who treats visitors from other countries and reads their records through verifiable health links. Fictional. Roles: Verifier. Goal. Read a visitor's record quickly and know it is genuine and that she is allowed to read it. Needs A clear answer: allowed, refused, or unknown A record she can trust, signed by a known issuer Frustrations Links that fail without saying why Kofi (auditor) Persona: an auditor who checks that every access under a data sharing agreement was allowed and its duties were done. Fictional. Roles: Auditor. Goal. Show, for any access, which consent and which agreement allowed it. Needs Provenance that cites the consent and its version Duty checks he can run himself Frustrations Logs that say who, but not why Lina (wallet holder) Persona: a 34-year-old teacher who keeps her health records in a personal health wallet on her phone and travels for work. Fictional. Roles: Holder, Consent Recorder. Goal. Share her health information only with the people who need it, for as long as they need it. Needs To see who can read her record, and to withdraw that at any time One link that works abroad as well as at home To know when her record was read, and by whom Frustrations Consent forms she cannot read back later Not knowing whether a withdrawal took effect Nurse Tomás (clinic nurse) Persona: a nurse at a community clinic who vaccinates, issues certificates, and records consent for patients who ask for help with the wallet. Fictional. Roles: Certificate Issuer, Consent Recorder. Goal. Issue certificates that are accepted wherever his patients go, without extra paperwork. Needs To record a patient's consent in one step, and show it back to them To know a certificate was issued correctly Frustrations Patients who were never asked what they agreed to Example systems System Roles Description --- --- --- Home health information exchange VHL Sharer, Consent Registry The health information exchange that holds Lina's record: it records her consent in its Consent Registry, generates her links and enforces consent when a link is redeemed. Security and privacy are part of each process in this guide, not a separate layer: Consent is enforced where the data is held. The VHL Sharer enforces the consent in its own Consent Registry (IHE PCF [ITI-108] ). A copy of a consent carried inside a document is evidence only. See Process A and Process C. No silent permit. A consent decision is permit , deny or unknown . A missing, expired or unreachable consent never gives permit . Trust is checked against a Trust Anchor. Signatures on links and certificates are verified against the trust list of an abstract Trust Anchor ( [ITI-YY2] ). The guide does not depend on one particular anchor. Decisions are recorded. Each access decision is recorded as W3C PROV-O provenance that cites Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId . Process G covers audit under a data sharing agreement. Revocation. Process H covers revoking and suspending access.
